item.title: A New Hip for $500 (and Why It Took Some Work)
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member's hip replacement cost him $500. The outpatient facility charge was a third of the hospital's. He says it took real effort.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A self-employed CrowdHealth member needed a hip replacement. By having it done at an outpatient surgery center instead of a hospital, the facility charge was one third of the hospital price, and he paid $500. He also turned down the first surgeon suggested and says his own effort was key. It isn't a magic fix, and he says so.

Joint replacements are planned. You see them coming for months. That makes them the best case for this model, because there's time to shop.

What happened?

CrowdHealth published the story of a self-employed man who'd started several businesses. He needed a new hip. It was his first big health event as a member.

It didn't go in a straight line. Getting an X-ray order from his regular doctor turned into a hassle. Then CrowdHealth suggested a surgery center in another city, and that first surgeon didn't meet his standards. So he pushed back.

They kept working at it together. They found a hip specialist from a well-regarded local group who operates at an outpatient surgery center near his home. That's a place built for same-day surgeries, separate from a hospital.

What did the bill look like?

The story doesn't give the total. It gives the two numbers that matter:

  • Facility charge at the surgery center: one third of the hospital price
  • What he paid: $500

Same new hip. One third the building cost.

A hospital is like a full-service hotel. You're paying for the lobby, the ballroom, and the 24-hour everything, whether you use them or not. An outpatient center is the clean roadside motel. You get the bed and the hot shower, and you don't pay for the ballroom.

Is there a second story?

Yes, and it isn't from CrowdHealth's own site. A member posted on an independent review site about a knee replacement. They paid $500, on top of a regular monthly cost of $176. CrowdHealth found a private surgery clinic about an hour from home. Physical therapy afterward was paid back in full. The second knee was already scheduled.

CrowdHealth's public results also show a hip replacement request that went out to 132 members.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

Found the fair price for the surgery, suggested surgeons, and kept looking when the first one wasn't a fit. Then the crowd funded everything over $500.

What's the honest part?

This member was blunt about it, and CrowdHealth printed it anyway, which I give them credit for. The piece says outright that CrowdHealth "isn't a magic fix."

He said his own effort made the difference. He asked questions. He turned down a surgeon. He kept pushing until the plan was right.

He also said it might not suit people with frequent health problems, or people who'd rather be passive about their care.

That's the trade in one sentence. You save a pile of money, and in exchange you act like the customer. If you want to hand over a card and never think about it again, a surgery like this will frustrate you.

There's a second catch for joints specifically. Worn-out hips and knees usually hurt for years before surgery. If you had symptoms or treatment in the five years before joining, that joint is a pre-existing condition. It wouldn't be shared for your first two years, and it's capped at $25,000 a year after that. A lot of people shopping for coverage because their knee already hurts will run into this.

And the knee member drove an hour. Not everyone can.

The takeaway

A new hip for $500 is real. So is the work behind it. For a planned surgery, the money is in where it's done, and an outpatient center can cost a fraction of a hospital. Bring your questions and your patience, and don't be afraid to say "not that surgeon."

Questions I get about this

Does CrowdHealth cover hip or knee replacement?

If the joint problem is new since you joined, yes. Members have reported paying $500 for a hip replacement and $500 for a knee replacement. If you had symptoms or treatment in the five years before joining, the pre-existing rule applies.

Why is an outpatient surgery center cheaper than a hospital?

Lower overhead. A surgery center does one kind of work and doesn't carry the cost of an ER or intensive care. One member's facility charge there was a third of the hospital's. The same idea is behind why cash prices beat insured prices.

Can I say no to the surgeon CrowdHealth suggests?

Yes. There are no networks, so you choose. One member turned down the first suggestion and worked with CrowdHealth to find another. The price still has to be near a fair local rate for the crowd to fund all of it.

item.title: When the Hospital Won't Budge and the Bill Goes to Collections
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: Some CrowdHealth members had hospital bills take six months to a year to negotiate and go to collections first. What happened, and what I'd do.
item.content:encoded:
In short: One CrowdHealth member's ER bill took more than six months to negotiate and went to collections after five. Another had a hospital bill sit in collections for about a year before it was paid. Both stayed members. Slow hospital negotiations are a real cost of this model, and you carry the stress while they happen.

Yesterday's ER stories were tidy. Today's aren't. If you're thinking about joining, you need both.

What happened?

Six months and a collections notice. A member had an unexpected ER visit. The hospital belonged to a system that flat-out wouldn't negotiate. CrowdHealth kept at it for more than six months.

After five-plus months, the unpaid balance was sent to collections. That means the hospital handed the debt to a company whose whole job is getting people to pay.

Within a couple of weeks of that, the balance finally came down by several hundred dollars and got settled. The member gave four stars and said the advocate personally checked in along the way. Their advice to new members: expect it to take months, and don't be shocked if a collections agency gets involved.

A year. A household wrote that one hospital bill went to collections while it was being negotiated and was finally paid after about a year. They described the negotiating style as stretching out the timeline to wear down the price. They wanted more updates. They've also referred two other families, so they haven't soured on it.

No sense of urgency. A third member, three stars, said they had to chase CrowdHealth for updates, and that nobody seemed in a hurry when bills were headed to collections. Their sharpest line was that the member keeps all the risk.

Why does this happen?

Because of how the bargaining works.

A hospital sends a huge first bill. CrowdHealth offers a fair cash price. The hospital says no. Then it's a waiting game. Whoever gets tired first gives in.

It's like haggling over a used car where the seller won't come down and you won't come up. The longer the car sits on the lot, the better your odds. But you're the one without a car in the meantime.

CrowdHealth replied to that three-star review. They admitted their communication needed to be better. They also said collections can actually help their bargaining position, that medical bills generally aren't reported to credit bureaus until they've gone unpaid for at least a year, and that they'd step in to clean up a credit report if a provider reported one during a negotiation. They said the app now shows which step each bill is on.

What's the honest part?

All of it. This whole post is the honest part.

When CrowdHealth holds firm on price, that helps every member. It's a big reason the monthly cost is low. But the letters and the phone calls go to one person: you. The bill has your name on it. If you're someone who loses sleep over a past-due notice, a year of them would be miserable.

I can't check the credit reporting claim for your situation, and rules like that can change. Don't take my word or theirs. Look up the current rules yourself if a bill of yours heads that way.

I'll also say this. In all three stories the bill did get paid. Nobody here got stuck with it. But "it worked out after a year" is a different promise than "it's handled."

What would I do?

Three things.

Ask your advocate for an update on a schedule, every two weeks, in writing. Don't wait to hear from them.

Keep every letter and every bill in one folder.

If you get a collections notice, send it to your advocate that day and ask what the plan is.

The takeaway

Most bills in CrowdHealth's results fund in about a week. A stubborn hospital can turn that into six months or a year, with collections letters in between. That's the price of having someone refuse to overpay. I think it's worth it. I'd want to know about it before I joined, not after.

Questions I get about this

Can a medical bill go to collections while CrowdHealth negotiates?

Yes. Several members have reported it, usually when a hospital refuses to negotiate. In the stories I read, the bills were eventually reduced and paid, after five months to a year. Keep your advocate updated on every notice you receive.

Will a bill in collections hurt my credit?

CrowdHealth says medical bills typically aren't reported to credit bureaus until unpaid for at least a year, and that it would help fix a report if a provider reported during negotiation. I can't verify that for your case. Check the current credit reporting rules yourself.

How long does hospital bill negotiation take?

Most bills fund in about a week once complete. Stubborn hospital bills can take months. I cover the worst case, where a bill isn't funded at all, in what if the crowd doesn't fund your bill.

item.title: The ER Bill: $4,142 Became $1,657 With One Phone Call
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A toddler's ER visit for croup was billed at $4,142.75. One phone call cut it 60% to $1,657.10. The dad paid $500 and CrowdHealth's crowd paid the rest.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A dad took his toddler to the ER for croup and got a bill for $4,142.75. CrowdHealth told him the hospital hadn't applied its self-pay discount. He called, and the bill dropped 60% to $1,657.10. He paid $500, the crowd funded the rest, and the money was in his account two weeks after he uploaded the bill.

ER visits are the most common "big" bill a normal family runs into. So here are three of them, with real numbers.

What happened?

The toddler with croup. A dad wrote on his own blog about his young son waking up in the night struggling to breathe. They went to the ER. It was croup, a swelling in the airway that's common in little kids. They were sent home a couple of hours later.

The bill showed up several weeks afterward: $4,142.75.

He uploaded it. Within a day or two, someone at CrowdHealth told him the hospital had overcharged and hadn't applied a self-pay discount. So he called the hospital and asked. They took 60% off right there on the phone.

The $10,000 visit. A self-employed mom wrote that her family of four dropped insurance this past year. Her husband landed in the ER in January. The visit was $10,000. The crowd paid all of it except their $500.

She also needed follow-up scans after a routine checkup. She figured insurance would have left her with around $4,000. On CrowdHealth, again, $500.

The overnight stay. A healthy member, four or five months in, had an ER visit and one night in the hospital. They paid the first $500. The biggest bill got negotiated to about half. Then they watched the crowd's money arrive in their account in small pieces: $62.45, $98.28, $76.13, $115.87.

What do the bills look like?

Here's the croup visit, start to finish:

  • Billed: $4,142.75
  • After the self-pay discount: $1,657.10
  • Dad paid: $500
  • Crowd funded: about $1,157
  • Time from upload to money in the bank: two weeks

I love that third story's detail about the small deposits. That's what a crowd looks like from the inside. It's a tip jar that fills up a few bills at a time until it covers the check.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

In the croup story, they spotted the overcharge. The dad made the call himself. That's worth being clear about. CrowdHealth told him what to ask. He did the asking.

In the overnight story, they coached the member on asking for self-pay discounts, negotiated the largest bill, and deposited the money once it was funded. That part took a day or two, maybe three.

What's the honest part?

That 60% discount wasn't a hard-fought deal. It was a standard discount the hospital gives anyone paying directly, if they ask. The hospital just didn't offer it. You could get that same discount with no membership in anything.

Which tells you two things. One, always ask. Two, the value here was someone who knew to tell him to ask.

ER bills also come in pieces. One member noted that the hospital, the doctor, and the lab each send their own, and every one has to be forwarded. A blogger whose husband went in with stomach pain got four separate bills. The small one was funded within days. The big one was still being negotiated when she wrote about it.

And CrowdHealth's founder has a warning I'll pass along. A children's hospital ER can charge far more than a regular one. He described a family billed more than $6,500 for a dehydrated child who needed fluids. For stitches or a fever, he says, go somewhere else if you safely can.

The takeaway

Three ER visits, three members who paid $500. The pattern I see: the first bill is too high, somebody asks, the bill drops, and the crowd splits what's left. The asking is the magic. Do it on any plan you have.

Questions I get about this

How much is an ER visit without insurance?

It varies a lot. In these member stories, one was $4,142.75 before a 60% discount and another was $10,000. Always ask for the self-pay price and an itemized bill. My full walk-through is in health sharing and the ER.

How do I get a self-pay discount at a hospital?

Call the billing office, say you're paying directly with no insurance, and ask what discount they offer. One dad got 60% off with a single call. I wrote out a script in how to negotiate a hospital bill yourself.

How long until I get paid back for an ER bill?

In these stories, between a few days and two weeks once the bill was approved. CrowdHealth's August 2026 average was 7.72 days from a complete bill to funds in the account. Larger hospital bills can take much longer to negotiate first.

item.title: Sick on a Sunday: A Doctor in 2 Minutes and a $6 Prescription
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member woke up sick on a Sunday and had a prescription in 2 minutes and 22 seconds. The medicine cost $6. How virtual visits work.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A CrowdHealth member woke up sick on a Sunday, opened the app, and had a prescription within 2 minutes and 22 seconds. The medicine cost $6. He felt better within a day. Virtual doctor visits are included on the standard membership, which makes the small, annoying illnesses the easiest part of the whole thing.

Most of what goes wrong with our health isn't a helicopter ride. It's a sore throat on a weekend when everything's closed.

What happened?

A member woke up feeling lousy on a Sunday. He didn't want to sit in an urgent care waiting room. So he opened the CrowdHealth app and tapped the option to talk to a doctor.

He timed it. Two minutes and 22 seconds later, he had a prescription sent to his local pharmacy.

The medicine cost him $6. He was back to normal within 24 hours.

That's the whole story. I like it because it's so small.

Are there other stories like it?

Plenty.

A newer member did their first virtual visit this summer. The prescription went to the pharmacy right after. They got a little confused turning in the bill, used the help tool in the app to sort it out, and the money was deposited quickly.

A mom of three wrote on her blog that one of her kids had a stomach bug. They did a virtual visit, got a prescription for the nausea, and the visit cost was refunded within a week.

Another member has used virtual care for travel medicine, a checkup, and a few small infections that needed antibiotics.

What does the bill look like?

On the standard membership, virtual primary care and urgent care visits are unlimited and can be turned in to the crowd. Starting January 1, 2027, the visit can be with any licensed provider, and up to $129 per visit can be shared without paying your $500 first.

The prescription is where a second lesson hides. CrowdHealth posted a short video where a mom tells this story. A young man with insurance needed a skin medicine. It took about three weeks to get it approved. Then at the counter it was $400. She called her own pharmacy, said she'd be paying cash, and asked the price. It was $26.

Same medicine. $400 with insurance and $26 without.

It's like the price on a concert ticket versus the price after the fees. Somehow the "help" made it cost more.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

Put a doctor in the app and a discount card in the member's pocket. That's it. No negotiating, no crowd, no forms.

What's the honest part?

A video visit can't do everything. A doctor on a screen can't listen to your lungs or look in your kid's ear. One member wanted blood work, and the virtual doctor wouldn't write the order, so they needed a second appointment. CrowdHealth's own complaints log from this August mentions a member whose virtual visit didn't meet their expectations.

The prescription rules are tight too. CrowdHealth doesn't share brand-name drugs when a generic exists. Ongoing medications are limited to a 12-month supply. And prescriptions have to be bought with CrowdHealth's discount tool to count. If you take an expensive medicine every month for the long haul, read health sharing and prescriptions before anything else.

Also, the cheaper membership option with the $15,000 commitment doesn't include funded virtual visits. This applies to the standard one.

One more caution. That first review is from 2022, and the service may work differently now. I can't promise you 2 minutes and 22 seconds.

The takeaway

For the everyday stuff, I don't need a crowd. I need a doctor I can reach on a Sunday and a pharmacy price that isn't a joke. A quick visit and a $6 prescription is the kind of boring win that adds up over a year.

item.title: Blood Work: $262 Last Year, $36 This Year
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member paid $262.13 for labs through insurance, then $36 the next year with a cash-price voucher. Why lab prices differ so much.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A CrowdHealth member paid $262.13 for lab work under their old insurance. The next year, using CrowdHealth's lab pricing, the same kind of blood work cost $36. Another member went from $300 or more to $60. Lab work is the easiest place to see how far cash prices sit below insured prices, with a couple of catches.

This one isn't dramatic. Nobody got flown anywhere. But I think it's the story most people will actually live, because everybody gets blood drawn sooner or later.

What happened?

A member wrote this spring about a simple before and after. Under their old big-name insurance plan, their labs cost $262.13. That was their share, with insurance.

This year on CrowdHealth, they paid $36.

They also said their doctor's exam was repaid within five days.

A second member told nearly the same story. They used to pay more than $300 out of pocket for labs. Using CrowdHealth's lab help, it was $60. That member gave four stars, not five, because the process was confusing at first and the app kept logging them out.

A third used two lab vouchers at a big national lab chain and said everything went smoothly.

Why is the gap so big?

Blood tests are cheap to run. The machine doesn't know who's paying. What changes is the price list.

When a lab bills through insurance, it often starts from a high sticker price. Your share gets figured from that, and if you haven't met your deductible, you pay most of it.

When you pay cash through a discount program, you get a price closer to what the test costs to run. I wrote a whole post on why the same blood test costs different amounts.

It's like a hotel minibar. The candy bar is $9 in the room and $1.50 at the gas station across the street. Same candy bar. One price counts on you not walking across the street.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

They gave these members a way to buy labs at the low price. You get an order from a doctor, CrowdHealth issues a voucher, and you take it to the lab.

That's it. No crowd funding involved. A $36 lab bill is way under the $500 mark, so this is just you paying a fair price.

What's the honest part?

Two catches, both from real reviews.

You need a doctor's order first. One member wanted routine blood work. They were told to do a telehealth visit to get the order. That doctor wouldn't write it. CrowdHealth couldn't issue the voucher without it. So the member needed a second appointment, and called the whole thing a runaround. CrowdHealth replied that this wasn't how it was supposed to go and said they'd look into it.

It doesn't work everywhere. A member in New York wrote that the lab vouchers don't apply in that state. If you live there, ask before you count on it.

And one more thing I want to be straight about. Paying $36 instead of $262 is great. It isn't the crowd paying for your labs. Routine blood work is on you, at a good price. If you want all your routine care paid for by someone else, this isn't that.

The takeaway

I get more excited about this story than the helicopter ones, honestly. A $226 difference on a basic blood draw, with nobody negotiating anything, tells you how padded the normal prices are. You don't even have to join anything to use the lesson. Ask what the cash price is. Every time.

How much does blood work cost without insurance?

Often far less than you'd think. One member paid $36 for labs that cost $262.13 through insurance the year before. Another paid $60 instead of $300 or more. Prices depend on the tests and the lab, so ask for the cash price up front.

Does CrowdHealth pay for routine lab work?

Not usually. Routine labs fall under your own costs, though you can use the yearly wellness allowance of up to $300 toward a checkup that includes them. What CrowdHealth gives you is access to low cash prices through lab vouchers.

Do lab vouchers work in every state?

No. A member in New York reported that the vouchers aren't available there. You also need an order from a doctor before a voucher can be issued. Ask your advocate how it works where you live before you rely on it.

item.title: The MRI That Took Two Weeks Instead of Months
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: One CrowdHealth member got a shoulder MRI in under two weeks at about half price. Another family saved over $5,000 on a cardiac MRI. How to shop for scans.
item.content:encoded:
In short: One member waited months for insurance to approve a shoulder MRI. On CrowdHealth it took under two weeks and cost about half the usual price. Another family saved more than $5,000 on a heart MRI for their son after their advocate found a better-priced place. Imaging is where shopping around pays off the most.

An MRI is a big scanning machine that takes pictures of the inside of your body. It's also one of the wildest-priced things in all of medicine. The same scan can cost a few hundred dollars or several thousand, depending on the building.

What happened?

The shoulder. A member needed a shoulder MRI and spent months trying to get it approved under their old coverage. After switching to CrowdHealth, they had the scan in under two weeks. The bill was about 50% lower than the going rate.

The son's heart. A family that was new to CrowdHealth needed a cardiac MRI for their son. Their advocate found a price that saved them more than $5,000 compared with what they'd been looking at. The same family had two wellness visits funded too.

The frozen shoulder. Another member, on a first-ever health event, needed an MRI and later a special injection for a frozen shoulder. The advocate found one provider that could do both.

The knee. A woman hurt her knee a few months after enrolling, while she still had her old insurance as a backup. Going through that insurance was going to cost her upwards of $10,000. CrowdHealth's team lined up the surgeon and the imaging quickly. Afterward her family dropped the insurance.

The extra $700. A member wrote in a members' group that he'd already gotten a discounted cash price on an MRI by asking. Then CrowdHealth got it another $700 lower.

What does the bill look like?

Here's why imaging is such a good deal to shop for. An MRI is the same machine doing the same thing everywhere. It isn't like surgery, where the surgeon's skill matters a lot. A standalone imaging center takes the same kind of picture a hospital does.

But hospitals often charge several times more. It's like bottled water. Same water at the gas station, the ballpark, and the airport. Wildly different prices, and the only thing that changed is where you were standing.

In CrowdHealth's public results, an MRI request is usually small. One went to 17 members. Several went to fewer than 10.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

Two things, and both are simple. They knew where the fair-priced places were, and there was no approval line to wait in.

That second one surprised me. With insurance, a scan often needs sign-off first, and that can take weeks. Here, you and your doctor decide you need a scan, you find a fair price, and you go.

What's the honest part?

If your MRI costs less than $500, it's all yours. Plenty of cash-price scans come in under that, so some members pay for imaging entirely out of pocket and the crowd never gets involved. You're still better off at the cash price. Just don't expect a check.

One member had a bad time with this exact thing. A testing bill came to $850, and they still paid $500 of it. They said it made them doubt whether a real emergency would go well. CrowdHealth's reply was that on a deductible plan they'd have paid the full $850. That's true, and I also understand why $350 back didn't feel like much.

The imaging also has to be for a new problem. A problem you had before joining can fall under the pre-existing rule.

The takeaway

For scans, the win usually isn't the crowd paying. It's finding out the scan costs a third of what you thought, and getting it next week instead of next season. Ask for the cash price at a standalone imaging center. That one habit will save you money on any plan.

Questions I get about this

How much does an MRI cost without insurance?

It depends hugely on where you go. Members report bills about 50% under the usual rate, and one family saved over $5,000 on a cardiac MRI by switching locations. Standalone imaging centers are usually much cheaper than hospitals. More in why cash prices beat insured prices.

Do I need approval before getting a scan on CrowdHealth?

item.title: His Heart Stopped for Four Minutes
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member's heart stopped for four minutes. A medical flight, a week in the ICU, triple bypass. What his wife says happened with the bills.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A member's heart stopped for more than four minutes at a public meeting. Medics revived him. He was flown to a hospital, spent a week in intensive care, and had triple bypass surgery. His wife called CrowdHealth the next day. When she wrote about it, many bills had been funded and others were still being negotiated.

This is about as big as a health event gets. It's also an unfinished story, and I'm going to tell it that way.

What happened?

A wife wrote a public review this spring about her husband. They'd had regular insurance their whole lives until about two years ago, when they switched to CrowdHealth. In two years they hadn't needed it once.

Then her husband's heart stopped at a meeting. He was gone for over four minutes. Medics on the scene brought him back. He was flown to the hospital, spent a week in the ICU, and then had triple bypass surgery. That's open-heart surgery to route blood around three blocked arteries.

She called CrowdHealth the day after it happened to ask what she needed to do.

What did CrowdHealth say?

Not to worry about any of it yet. Focus on him.

That same message shows up in more than one of the scary stories I read. When you're in a hospital hallway, the money question is sitting on your chest. Somebody telling you "that part can wait" is worth a lot.

After that, the team walked the two of them through the process. They'd never turned in a bill before, so they needed the hand-holding.

What did the bill look like?

She didn't share numbers. She did list what was coming: the medical flight, the ICU, the surgeries, and more.

She said they were "beyond nervous" about whether it would all get paid. Two years of paying in, never taking out, and then the biggest possible bill all at once.

By the time she wrote, many of the bills had been crowdfunded. CrowdHealth was still negotiating others.

Is there a second story like this?

Yes. A man who'd lost the insurance he had through work joined CrowdHealth, then had a stroke that led to heart surgery. His path to treatment ran through several hospital systems and took almost a year.

He said his advocate worked between those hospitals for him, and that other members' money got him through surgery and back on his feet. No dollar figures in that one either.

What's the honest part?

Neither of these reviews has a final number, and the first one wasn't finished. "Many bills funded, others in negotiation" is good news. It's not the same as "done."

Heart events also raise the hardest version of the pre-existing question. If you'd been treated for a heart problem in the five years before joining, a later heart event could fall under that rule. High blood pressure and high cholesterol by themselves are exempt, which helps a lot of people my age.

And think about that wife for a second. For weeks, those bills were arriving at her house with her name on them. Nobody had signed a contract promising to pay them. She trusted a track record. It held. I just don't want to make that sound smaller than it was.

The takeaway

Two years of paying in. One catastrophic week. A phone call the next morning, and someone saying "take care of him first." That's the moment the whole thing either works or it doesn't. For this couple, by her account, it was working.

item.title: Two Hernia Surgeries, Two Very Different Stories
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: One CrowdHealth member had hernia surgery in three weeks. Another was quoted $12,000 to $15,000 and offered $8,000. The fair price rule explains both.
item.content:encoded:
In short: One CrowdHealth member had hernia surgery within three weeks of his first appointment, with staff helping him find the surgeon. Another was quoted $12,000 to $15,000 locally, was told CrowdHealth would fund $8,000, and was pointed to a doctor five hours away. The difference is a rule called fair pricing, and you should understand it before you join.

Same surgery. Same company. One five-star review and one two-star review. I think you learn more from putting them side by side than from either one alone.

What happened in the good one?

A married man had recently left a big-name insurance plan for CrowdHealth. He'd had a hernia fixed on the other side four years earlier, back when he was insured, so he knew the drill.

This time he noticed a bulge that grew and started to hurt. Three people at CrowdHealth helped him find a surgeon and walked him through the steps in the app. He had outpatient surgery at a large hospital system within three weeks of his consultation. In at 7 in the morning, home by 10.

He wrote his review that same day, and said the crowd funded everything.

What happened in the bad one?

A different member also needed hernia surgery. This is someone who doesn't get paid for time off work.

CrowdHealth sent this member to two doctors. Each consult cost $300. Both doctors quoted the surgery at $12,000 to $15,000. CrowdHealth said both prices were too high compared with what it considers fair, and that it would fund $8,000.

Then they suggested a doctor five hours away.

By the time the review went up, this member had spent $600 on visits, lost two days of pay, waited months on estimates, and still hadn't had the surgery. The review was kind about the advocate. The rep was great, it said, "but his hands are tied."

Why the difference?

It comes down to how CrowdHealth decides what to fund.

They work out a fair price for a procedure in your area. If your provider's price is close to that, the whole bill goes to the crowd. If it's well above, the crowd funds up to the fair amount, and the gap is yours unless you find a cheaper provider.

Picture a friend who offers to pay for your tires. He'll cover what tires cost at a normal shop. If you pick the dealership that charges double, he'll still chip in the normal-shop amount. Reasonable for him. Frustrating for you if the dealership is the only shop in town.

CrowdHealth replied to this member publicly. They explained the fair pricing, offered to fund travel costs, and said the consult fees could be turned in separately. In a reply to a similar review, they said they don't ask members to travel past the nearest big city for procedures under $10,000.

What's the honest part?

Where you live matters a lot. If your area has a few surgery centers competing for patients, you'll probably be the first member. If one hospital system owns your whole region, you could be the second.

There's no way around this from where I sit. The same rule that keeps my monthly cost low is the rule that left that member stuck. Members pay less because the crowd refuses to pay the inflated price. Somebody has to be the one standing in the doctor's office when that refusal happens.

I'll also say the first review was written the day of surgery. The final bills hadn't come yet.

The takeaway

Before you join, find out what your options are near home. Are there independent surgery centers nearby? Do they post cash prices? If the answer is "one big hospital and nothing else," know that you may be asked to drive, or to cover a gap. That's a real cost, and it belongs in your math.

Questions I get about this

What is CrowdHealth's fair price rule?

CrowdHealth compares your provider's price to what it considers a fair local price. Bills priced 20% or more above that get flagged, and the crowd may fund only up to the fair amount. You can switch providers, travel, or pay the difference. It's one of the questions in what to ask before you switch.

Will I have to travel for surgery?

Sometimes. CrowdHealth says it's rare and mostly affects members in small towns, and that it can help with travel costs. One member was asked to consider a doctor five hours away after two local quotes came in high.

How do I find a fairly priced surgeon?

Ask your advocate for options before you book anything, and ask each office for a written cash price. Independent surgery centers are often far cheaper than hospitals for the same procedure. I walk through the asking part in the cash price secret.

item.title: Cancer, a Few Months After Joining
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member was diagnosed with stage 4 melanoma months after joining, facing $100,000 treatments. What was funded, and the honest limits.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A dad joined CrowdHealth and was diagnosed with stage 4 melanoma two or three months later. He was told each treatment cost over $100,000, every three weeks. He says a surgery of about $17,000 was funded right after it was done, and a later biopsy was funded before it happened. Scans afterward showed no sign of cancer.

This is the question I get most. "Fine, it works for a broken arm. What about cancer?" So here's a cancer story, with the parts that should give you comfort and the parts that shouldn't.

What happened?

A married dad with a family of four left a job that had given his family cheap insurance. When he priced a plan on his own, it was about $2,200 a month with $120 copays. His doctor's cash price for a visit was $95. He joined CrowdHealth instead.

Two or three months later, a growth on his head that had been removed and tested as fine came back. This time it grew fast and hurt. He got three different answers from three rounds of testing. The last one, after a second opinion, was melanoma, a serious skin cancer. He says stage 4.

Treatment was planned for every three weeks, for up to two years.

Then came surgery to take out what was left of the tumor and two lymph nodes. The nodes were clear. A scan a couple of months later showed no evidence of cancer.

What did the bill look like?

The first number he heard from his cancer doctor was $20,000 per treatment. Then a nurse corrected it: more than $100,000 per treatment. Every three weeks.

The surgery was about $17,000 by his memory.

He didn't give totals for what was negotiated or funded, so I can't tell you those. CrowdHealth's list of its largest funded bills does include a stage 4 melanoma case at $272,972. I can't confirm that's him.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

For the surgery, they had him get a written estimate ahead of time and send it in. They funded from that. He says the surgery was funded right after it was done. A later lung biopsy was funded before it even happened.

He also said nothing had to wait on an approval, and nobody rationed his scans.

Early on, a rep told him he'd be handled the same way any other member would, as long as it met the rules.

What's the honest part?

Several things, and they matter.

He was scared it wouldn't count. He'd only been a member for a couple of months. And there had been that earlier growth. The story doesn't explain how that sat with the rule about symptoms before joining. It was funded. I can't tell you exactly why the rule didn't block it, and I won't pretend to know.

His cancer doctor was alarmed when he said he had no insurance. Expect that reaction. You'll have to explain yourself in a lot of offices.

Other cancer stories are less tidy. A husband wrote that the community covered "most" of the costs of his wife's cancer treatment. Most, not all. A woman with a new breast cancer diagnosis said she felt more in control of her treatment, and also that she was doing more legwork getting estimates. Her treatment hadn't started yet.

Long treatments are the weak spot. CrowdHealth's guide limits ongoing prescriptions to a 12-month supply and excludes some high-cost drugs. One independent writer who joined pointed out that a condition needing expensive care forever is the real risk in this model. I think he's right.

The takeaway

A man got a terrifying diagnosis a few months after joining, and by his account the crowd came through on six-figure treatments. That's the best evidence I've found that this works for the big stuff. It's also one person's story, chosen by the company, with questions I can't answer. For cancer in particular, I'd read the member guide twice and ask hard questions before betting my family on it.

Questions I get about this

Does CrowdHealth cover cancer treatment?

A new cancer found after you join is an eligible health event, and CrowdHealth's published list of large funded bills includes several cancers from $143,000 to $272,000. Funding isn't guaranteed, and there are limits on long-term prescriptions and experimental treatment. Read the guide before relying on it.

What if I'm diagnosed right after joining?

New conditions are eligible from day one. But if you had symptoms in the five years before joining, the pre-existing rule can apply even without a diagnosis. That's the gray area. See pre-existing conditions and health sharing.

Do I pay $500 for every treatment?

No. Everything tied to one condition is one health event, so you pay $500 once for that cancer, not per visit and not per year. That's very different from a deductible that starts over every January. I compare them in the $500 you pay vs the deductible you don't.

item.title: The $10,000 Bill the Crowd Never Saw
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A couple's $10,000 bill was denied by CrowdHealth over a symptom from before they joined. How the five-year, two-year pre-existing rule really works.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A couple about seven months into CrowdHealth had a $10,000 bill denied. The reason was a symptom that had been checked by a doctor before they joined. Under CrowdHealth's rules, anything diagnosed, treated, or showing symptoms in the five years before joining isn't shared for two years, and is capped at $25,000 a year after that.

I promised the bad stories too. This is the first one, and it's the rule that trips up more people than any other.

What happened?

A woman wrote a one-star public review about a claim for her household. They'd been members for almost seven months. They were paying about $110 a month in fees, plus $200 to $300 a month toward other members' bills.

Then they had a health problem that produced a $10,000 bill. CrowdHealth had them fill out forms describing the issue. In those forms was a symptom that had come up before, one a doctor had looked at before they joined.

The bill was denied. They appealed. The appeal was denied too. The bill was never sent to the crowd at all.

Why was it denied?

Here is the rule, as plainly as I can put it.

If you had a condition in the five years before joining, it isn't shared during your first two years. In year three and after, it's shared up to $25,000 a year.

The part people miss is what "had a condition" means. It isn't only a diagnosis. It also covers symptoms, things a doctor suspected, and anything you were treated for. So a symptom that got looked at and never got a name can still count.

CrowdHealth replied publicly to her review. They said the rule is on the sign-up page and in the member guide, and they offered to help find a lower-cost way to get the care.

Think of it like buying a used car "as is." Anything already rattling when you drove it off the lot is yours to fix. The warranty is for what breaks later.

How often does this happen?

More than I expected, and CrowdHealth publishes it. Each month, about 3% to 5% of submitted bills are ruled not eligible. In August 2026 it was 4.94%.

Their results list the reasons, and some are brutal in how small they are. One note says a member's symptoms started three days before their start date. Another says one month before. Another says medical records showed three weeks of symptoms before joining.

Another member wrote that an event of theirs was flagged as previously diagnosed when they say it wasn't, and it was still unresolved when they posted.

What's the honest part?

I think the rule itself is fair. A crowd can't work if people join the week after they find a lump. Somebody has to pay for that, and it'd be the rest of us.

But fair and painless aren't the same thing. This couple thought they were covered and found out otherwise holding a $10,000 bill. Whether they misread the rule or it wasn't explained well, the result was the same for them.

To her credit, the reviewer added that CrowdHealth might still be a good fit for a pregnancy or a sudden emergency. That's about right. This is built for new things, not old things.

There are two exceptions worth knowing. High blood pressure and high cholesterol are exempt from the rule. And brand-new accidents and new illnesses are eligible from day one.

The takeaway

Before you join, sit down and list every doctor visit and every nagging symptom from the last five years. Assume anything on that list is on you for two years. If that list has something expensive on it, CrowdHealth may not be your tool right now, and I'd tell you that to your face.

Questions I get about this

What counts as a pre-existing condition on CrowdHealth?

Anything diagnosed, treated, suspected, or showing symptoms in the five years before you joined. It doesn't need a formal diagnosis. Those conditions aren't shared in years one and two, then are capped at $25,000 a year. Full breakdown in CrowdHealth and pre-existing conditions.

Can I appeal a denied bill?

You can ask for a review. In this member's case the appeal was also denied. CrowdHealth isn't insurance, so there's no state regulator to take it to afterward. That's a real difference, and I talk about it in health sharing vs insurance.

Who should not join because of this rule?

Anyone who needs steady, costly care for something they already have. A guaranteed insurance plan is the better fit for that person. I wrote the whole list in who health sharing is wrong for.

item.title: Kidney Stones: Funded in Under Two Weeks
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member needed kidney stone surgery, paid up front, and was repaid in under two weeks. What it shows about paying first and getting paid back.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A fit business owner, eight months into CrowdHealth, needed surgery for kidney stones. He paid the bills himself first, turned them in, and the crowd paid him back in less than two weeks. Kidney stones are one of the most common requests in CrowdHealth's public results, with about 60 funded requests over roughly two years.

Folks who've had a kidney stone tend to describe it the same way: the worst pain of their life, out of nowhere. It's a classic "healthy people get surprised too" problem.

What happened?

A man who runs a few businesses and takes his fitness seriously wrote a public review this summer. He'd been a member for eight months and hadn't needed anything.

Then the stones hit. He described severe pain, and he ended up needing surgery. He was clear that the surgery cost a lot.

He paid the bills out of his own pocket. Then he sent them to CrowdHealth. The crowd funded them in less than two weeks.

A second member, with a family and more than three years in, wrote about an ER trip for a kidney stone. CrowdHealth negotiated the bills, and the community funded what was left after the member's $500.

A third member wrote about a daughter who was in and out of the hospital with several procedures for kidney stones, and how much help they got turning in all those bills.

What does the bill look like?

None of these three members shared a dollar amount, so I'm not going to invent one.

What I can show you is how common this is. CrowdHealth posts its funding requests each month, with the state and the type of event. Over about two years, I count roughly 60 requests for kidney stones. One was sent to 43 members. Another, for a stone removal, went to 35. An ER visit for stones went to 18.

That tells you something useful. A kidney stone bill is big to one person and small to a crowd. A few dozen people chip in and it's done. It's like splitting the check when one friend's car breaks down. Thirty-five people throwing in is a non-event for each of them.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

For the first member, mostly one thing: paid him back fast. He covered the bills, uploaded them, and the money came back in under two weeks.

For the second, they negotiated the ER bills down before anything went to the crowd.

What's the honest part?

He had to pay first. That's the piece people don't love, and they're right to notice it. If you get hit with a surgery bill, you need either cash, a card with room on it, or a payment plan with the hospital while you wait.

This is why I keep saying an emergency fund and CrowdHealth go together. I wrote about building the first $1,000 for exactly this kind of week.

CrowdHealth says that for bigger bills it can negotiate, and sometimes fund, before you pay. So ask your advocate before you put a large bill on a card.

One more thing. Kidney stones tend to come back. If you had stones or symptoms in the five years before joining, a new stone could be treated as a pre-existing condition and not shared in your first two years. A first-ever stone for a new member is a different story.

The takeaway

A healthy guy got blindsided, paid for surgery, and was made whole in under two weeks. That's the system working the plain, boring way it's supposed to. The price of admission is being able to float the bill for a little while.

The parents also described a stretch of real fear before they knew it would be funded. They wondered if joining had been a mistake. It worked out. They didn't know that while they were living it.

item.title: One Heart Procedure, Three Prices: $83,655, $44,000, and $22,000
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member was quoted $83,655, $44,000, and $22,000 for the same heart procedure. He paid $500 and 150 members funded the rest in 3 days.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A member needed a heart rhythm procedure. His local hospital quoted $83,655. A hospital 90 miles away quoted $44,000. One a few states away quoted $22,000. With travel, the whole thing came to about $30,000. He paid $500, and 150 members funded the other $29,500 in three days.

If I told you a gallon of milk cost $8 at one store and $2 at another, you'd drive. This is that, with a heart.

What happened?

CrowdHealth published this couple's story back in 2022. He's self-employed. His wife had lost her job, and the family's insurance went with it. They'd joined CrowdHealth a few months earlier and weren't sure yet that a crowd of strangers would really show up.

Then one day, mid-workout, his heart rate shot up to about 230 beats a minute and wouldn't come back down. The ER figured out what it was: a fast heart rhythm problem. The fix is a procedure where a doctor goes in and corrects the spot causing the trouble.

It worked. He was cleared with no restrictions afterward.

What did the bill look like?

This is the part that made my jaw drop. Same procedure, three hospitals:

  • Local hospital: $83,655
  • A big-city hospital about 90 miles away: $44,000
  • A hospital a few states away: $22,000

That's not a typo. The far one was about a quarter of the local one.

So they went. Plane tickets, three hotel nights, a driver, meals, and the procedure came to about $30,000 all in. That was more than $50,000 under the local quote, even after paying for the trip.

He paid his $500. CrowdHealth asked 150 members to fund the remaining $29,500. The money was there in three days, before the procedure.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

They did the shopping. They took the quotes, called other hospitals, and found the $22,000 one. They booked the travel and lined up a local person to drive the couple around once they landed. Then they sent the request to the crowd.

This is the part I love. I've never heard of an insurance company calling three hospitals to find a member a better price. Why would they? It isn't their job.

What's the honest part?

He had to get on a plane for a heart procedure. That's a real ask. Some folks can't travel, or don't want to be far from home for something scary. In a true emergency, you don't get this choice at all. This worked because he was stable enough to plan.

The couple also said they were nervous the whole time. They hadn't seen the crowd come through yet. I think that's normal, and I'd rather tell you than pretend it feels like a sure thing.

Two more notes. This happened in 2022, and CrowdHealth's pricing has changed since then. And the written story and the video description don't match on a couple of small details, like whether 150 or 152 members chipped in. I used the written version.

CrowdHealth says being asked to travel for a big procedure is rare. Its founder put it at around 10 times in 60,000 bills, mostly for folks in very small towns.

The takeaway

Same procedure, $83,655 or $22,000, depending on the building. Prices for the same care can be four times apart, and most of us never find out because nobody shows us the menu. Having someone make those calls is worth a lot.

Will CrowdHealth make me travel for surgery?

Usually not. CrowdHealth says travel requests are rare, roughly 10 in 60,000 bills. But funding is based on a fair price for your area, so if local quotes come in far above that, you may be asked to look farther away or cover the gap. That trade-off is real, and I cover it in what if the crowd doesn't fund your bill.

Because prices aren't posted and most patients never ask. Each hospital sets its own sticker price, and the people paying usually aren't the people choosing. I dug into this in why cash prices beat insured prices.

In this story, three days. Across everything, CrowdHealth's August 2026 results showed an average of 7.72 days from a complete bill to money in the member's account. Big, messy hospital bills can take a lot longer to negotiate first.

item.title: The $35,000 Appendix That Cost $500
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A CrowdHealth member's emergency appendectomy was quoted at $35,000, reduced to $10,600, and cost him $500. What that says about hospital sticker prices.
item.content:encoded:
In short: One member's emergency appendectomy was first quoted at $35,000. CrowdHealth got it reduced to $10,600, he paid his $500, and other members shared the rest. Another member, a doctor, was billed about $50,000 for nine hours in the ER and operating room. Appendix bills are a great lesson in how far apart the sticker price and the real price can be.

Your appendix doesn't schedule anything. It just goes. That makes it a good test of any health plan, because you can't shop around while you're doubled over.

What happened?

CrowdHealth published the story of a married couple who had waited six or seven months before deciding to join. They'd been paying about $450 a month for insurance they rarely used.

Then the husband needed an emergency appendectomy. That's the surgery to take out an appendix before it bursts.

What did the bill look like?

Here are the numbers from their story:

  • First quote: $35,000
  • After it was reduced: $10,600
  • What he paid: $500
  • The rest: shared by other members

That first number isn't a lie exactly. It's a starting bid. Think of a rug at a street market with a $900 tag on it. The seller knows nobody pays $900. The tag is there for whoever doesn't ask.

Is that kind of bill normal?

A second member's public review backs it up. This one was a physician. They described nine hours total, from the ER to the operating room to home, and a bill of about $50,000. They said CrowdHealth had them covered. They didn't say what they paid or what the bill came down to, so I won't guess.

And CrowdHealth's own list of big funded bills includes one for appendicitis that reached $333,943. The list doesn't say what made that one so large.

So the same body part can run $10,600 or $333,000 depending on how it goes and who's asking. That range is the whole reason I want somebody on my side.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

In the first story, they got the price cut from $35,000 to $10,600 using self-pay pricing. Self-pay just means you're paying directly instead of through an insurance company. Hospitals will often take far less from a direct payer, because they get paid faster and skip the paperwork fight.

Then the crowd covered everything above the member's $500.

The couple also said the advocates later pointed them to a doctor who only takes self-pay patients, and they liked him a lot.

What's the honest part?

You don't get the discount at the front desk. In an emergency you get the care, and the negotiating happens afterward, with the bill in your name. That takes some nerve the first time. I'd be lying if I said opening a $35,000 envelope feels fine just because you know the plan.

The second story left out the ending. A doctor saying "they had me covered" is encouraging. It isn't a receipt.

And this first story was chosen and published by CrowdHealth. They pick the good ones. Keep that in mind, the same way you would with any company's testimonials.

The takeaway

A $35,000 quote became $10,600, and the member paid $500. The lesson isn't that surgery is cheap. It's that the first price is rarely the real one, and it helps to have someone whose job is to ask.

How much does an appendectomy cost without insurance?

It varies wildly. In the member stories I found, one was quoted $35,000 and reduced to $10,600, another was billed about $50,000, and the largest on CrowdHealth's published list reached $333,943. The first quote is a starting point, which is why I always ask for the cash price.

On the standard membership, you pay the first $500 of an eligible health event. The surgery, the ER visit, the scans, and the follow-ups for that same problem all count as one event. Anything above $500 goes to the crowd after the bill is negotiated.

CrowdHealth's team does for larger bills, and your care advocate walks you through it. I wrote about that job in what a care advocate actually does. You can also do it yourself with my hospital bill script.

item.title: A Toddler, a Medevac, and $30,000 in Bills
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: A dad's toddler was medevacked to a pediatric ICU. Over $30,000 in bills, cut by more than half, and he paid his $500 CrowdHealth commitment.
item.content:encoded:
In short: A dad's 18-month-old son couldn't breathe and was medevacked to a pediatric ICU 90 minutes away. The bills came to more than $30,000. CrowdHealth helped negotiate them down by more than half, the crowd shared what was left, and the dad paid his $500. A couple of bills were still open when he wrote about it.

This is the story that made me want to write this whole series. It's every parent's bad night.

What happened?

A dad wrote a public review earlier this year about his 18-month-old son. The boy had a rough cough and started struggling to breathe. They rushed to the ER in the middle of the night. After about 12 hours on oxygen, the doctors said he needed a pediatric ICU, and it was an hour and a half away. So he went by medevac.

The dad says he asked along the way what all this would cost. He was told not to worry about it. Any parent would have said yes to that ride anyway.

His son got better. Then the mail started coming.

What did the bills look like?

More than $30,000 worth, in several envelopes. That's how hospital billing works. The ER sends one. The medevac company sends one. The ICU sends one. The doctors send their own. It's like a restaurant where the cook, the waiter, and the dishwasher each mail you a separate check.

Here's how the dad says it shook out:

  • Billed: over $30,000
  • After negotiating: cut by more than 50%
  • What he paid: his $500 member commitment
  • The rest: shared by other members

He also said some of the big bills were paid back to him before his own payment to the hospital was even due.

What did CrowdHealth actually do?

Two things. First, they negotiated. A hospital's first bill is a sticker price, like the number on a new car window. Almost nobody pays it. Insurance companies don't. Cash payers shouldn't either. I wrote about that in the cash price secret.

Second, once the price was fair, they sent the bills out to the crowd. Other members each chipped in a small amount, and the money landed in his account.

He also mentioned something that shows up in a lot of member reviews. When he had a "what if" question, a real person answered the same day or the next. No hold music.

What's the honest part?

A few things, and the dad said most of them himself.

It wasn't finished. A couple of bills were still being worked on two months later. Big events take a while to close out.

You are the one holding the bills while that happens. Your name is on them, not CrowdHealth's.

And his situation fit the rules. A sudden illness in a healthy kid is exactly what this is built for. He listed the limits in his own review: conditions you already had aren't shared for the first two years, you have to join before a pregnancy, and people 65 and up or who use tobacco can't join.

Why this one sticks with me

His old insurance plan cost about $500 a month just for him, with a $4,000 deductible. He figured a family plan would have run about $1,500 a month with a $12,000 deductible. A deductible is the amount you pay yourself before insurance pays a dime. So on that plan, this same night could have cost him $12,000 on top of the monthly bill.

Instead it was $500. That's the whole pitch, in one bad night.

The takeaway

When a kid can't breathe, nobody shops for prices. The shopping happens after, and this dad had someone doing it for him. More than $30,000 billed, cut by more than half, $500 out of pocket. Not finished yet when he wrote it, and not guaranteed. But it worked the way he was told it would.

In this member's story, the medevac was part of the health event and its bill was handled with the others. One limit I do know: CrowdHealth's member guide says international air ambulance is not eligible. Read the current guide, because it's the rulebook.

Go. Get care first and sort out the money later. No plan of any kind is worth a delay when someone can't breathe. I wrote a step-by-step for this in health sharing and the ER.

In short: I'm a fan of CrowdHealth because it's simple enough to explain on a napkin: about $60 a month per person, a share of other members' bills, and $500 out of my pocket per health event. This month I'm retelling real member situations, one kind per day, good and bad, with no names, so you can see how it works when something actually happens.

I'll say it plainly. I'm a CrowdHealth fanboy. My family of four has used it since 2022, and I'll happily talk your ear off about it.

But me liking something isn't proof of anything. So this month I'm doing it differently. Every day for the rest of October I'm taking one real health situation that a real member went through, and walking through what happened. A baby. A broken ankle. An appendix. Cancer. And a handful where it went sideways, because those are real too.

Why am I such a fan?

Three reasons, and none of them are fancy.

I can explain it. I pay $60 a month per person to CrowdHealth for the help: the advocate, the bill negotiating, the app. (That fee goes to $65 in January 2027.) On top of that I chip in toward other members' bills each month. That part moves around, and it has a ceiling. If something happens to one of us, we pay the first $500 of that health event. The crowd shares the rest.

The money goes to people. When I chip in, it goes to another member with a real bill. Not to a building with a fountain in the lobby.

They show their work. CrowdHealth publishes monthly results. In August 2026 members turned in 3,870 bills, and the average bill took 7.72 days to fund once the paperwork was complete. They also publish a complaints log. I've never seen an insurance company do that.

It's like a potluck. Everybody brings a dish. When it's your turn to be hungry, there's food. Nobody promises you a plate in writing, but more than 53,000 funded bills in, people keep showing up with casseroles.

How am I telling these stories?

I pulled together public member reviews, CrowdHealth's own published member stories, and its monthly results. Then I set some rules for myself:

  • No names, no towns, nothing that points at a person. These are people's medical lives.
  • My own words. I retell what happened. I don't copy it.
  • Real numbers only. If a member didn't say what something cost, I won't guess.
  • The bad ones go in too. Slow bills, denied bills, paperwork headaches. About one post in four this month is a story where it didn't go great.
  • I say where each story came from, at the bottom of every post.

One more honest note. I can't verify a stranger's review. When a story comes from CrowdHealth's own site, remember they picked it. I'll tell you which is which.

What should you know before any of this?

CrowdHealth is not insurance. Nobody is legally required to pay your bill. Members are responsible for their own bills in the end, and the crowd has funded more than 99% of the eligible ones.

"Eligible" is doing real work in that sentence. Conditions you had symptoms of in the five years before joining aren't shared for your first two years, and they're capped at $25,000 a year after that. Dental work, most mental health care, and ongoing brand-name prescriptions aren't shared. You can't join at 65 or older, or if you use tobacco. I wrote up who health sharing is wrong for if you want that list first.

The short answer

A strong track record is evidence about the past. It's not a contract about your future. The distinction matters more than anything else on this page, so let me put it plainly.

item.title: CrowdHealth and Pre-Existing Conditions: The Real Rules
item.dc:creator: David Dewese
item.description: CrowdHealth funds nothing for pre-existing conditions in years 1-2, then $25,000/yr from year 3. The 5-year window, and the cholesterol and blood pressure exemption.
item.content:encoded:
In short: Anything documented, diagnosed, symptomatic, suspected, or treated within five years of joining CrowdHealth gets no funding in years one and two, then up to $25,000 a year from year three on. High cholesterol and high blood pressure are explicitly exempt. If you have a real ongoing condition, this rule is usually the whole answer, and the answer is often no.

This is the rule that decides it for most people, and it's the one most reviews gloss over. So I'm going to give you CrowdHealth's actual language, not my summary of it, and then tell you what I think it means for you.

I'm a member. My family of four has used CrowdHealth since 2022. I'd rather you read this and walk away than join and find out in an emergency room.

What the rule actually says

CrowdHealth's term is Previously Documented, Diagnosed, or Symptomatic conditions. Their guidelines say the crowd welcomes members with varied health backgrounds, but there are limits on funding health events tied to these conditions.

Here's the shape of it:

  • The window is five years before you join.
  • It covers anything diagnosed, documented, symptomatic, suspected, or treated in that window. Note "suspected." You don't need a formal diagnosis for this to apply.
  • Years one and two of membership: not eligible for funding. Not reduced. Not eligible.
  • Year three and after: a $25,000 per year crowdfunding cap for anything related to those conditions.

Their own examples, and they're clear the list isn't exhaustive: asthma, congenital conditions, diabetes, genetic disorders, heart conditions, sleep apnea.

One of those is about to get its own rule. Starting January 1, 2027, Type 2 diabetes care won't be eligible for crowdfunding on the standard membership at all, even for a new diagnosis. Members who want help with it move to a separate CrowdHealth program called Exit Diabetes.

Children who join CrowdHealth at birth are excepted from the congenital condition limit.

The exemption almost nobody mentions

High cholesterol and high blood pressure are not subject to these limits.

I want to put that on its own line, because those two are the single most common thing a 45-year-old is quietly worried about when they read a pre-existing clause. If your doctor has you on a statin or a blood pressure pill and you assumed that disqualified you, it doesn't.

I've read a lot of CrowdHealth write-ups. Almost none of them mention this. It's in the guidelines.

What "suspected" means for you, practically

This is the part I'd think hardest about.

The rule doesn't require a diagnosis. If something was symptomatic, or a doctor suspected it and wrote it down, it's inside the window. That means the honest question isn't "what am I diagnosed with." It's "what is in my chart from the last five years."

Most people don't actually know. So before you cancel anything:

  1. Request your records from your primary care doctor for the last five years.
  2. Read what's written there, including notes about things that turned out to be nothing.
  3. Ask CrowdHealth directly, in writing, about anything you find. Get the answer in writing too.

That third step is the important one. Do not rely on a blog post, mine included, for a question this specific to your body.

What this rule is actually for

It's easy to read this as the company weaseling. I don't think that's what it is, and it's worth understanding the logic, because it tells you what the product is.

CrowdHealth isn't insurance, and it isn't legally required to take all comers the way an ACA plan is. Its costs stay low because the crowd is mostly funding unexpected things. If somebody could join the month after a serious diagnosis and have the crowd pick up an ongoing treatment, the monthly ask for everybody else would climb until the thing stopped working.

That's the trade. It's cheap partly because it doesn't do this. Knowing that doesn't help you if you're the one with the condition, but it does tell you the rule isn't going to get quietly relaxed.

Who this rule disqualifies

Be honest with yourself here:

  • Anyone with a chronic condition needing ongoing treatment. Two years of nothing, then a $25,000 annual ceiling, is not coverage for diabetes or a heart condition. It's a partial subsidy starting two years from now.
  • Anyone in the middle of a workup. If you're currently being investigated for something, it's symptomatic or suspected now, which puts it in the window.
  • Anyone who'd be gambling. If you're hoping the rule won't be applied to you, don't join. It'll be applied.

If that's you, the honest answer is a real insurance plan, and I'd rather say so than take the referral. There's more in who health sharing is wrong for.

Who it doesn't disqualify

  • Reasonably healthy people whose charts are boring.
  • People managing only cholesterol or blood pressure, per the exemption above.
  • People whose past issue is more than five years back and has stayed quiet.
  • Anything genuinely new that happens after you join. That's the main event, and it's funded normally.

The part I have to say

Even outside these rules, CrowdHealth is not insurance. There's no legal guarantee any bill gets funded, and no state regulator to call if one doesn't. The record is strong, 53,877 bills funded at a 99.8 percent rate, but a record is not a promise.

The whole picture, including costs and the monthly cap, is on my CrowdHealth guide.

Questions I get about this

Does CrowdHealth cover pre-existing conditions?

Not in years one and two. From year three, up to $25,000 a year for conditions documented, diagnosed, symptomatic, suspected, or treated within five years of joining.

How far back does CrowdHealth look?

Five years before your join date.

Does high blood pressure disqualify me from CrowdHealth?

No. High blood pressure and high cholesterol are explicitly exempt from the previously documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic limits.

What if I was never formally diagnosed?

The rule covers conditions that were symptomatic or suspected, not just diagnosed. Pull your medical records and ask CrowdHealth in writing before you join.

Is asthma a pre-existing condition for CrowdHealth?

Asthma is on their own list of examples, so yes, if it was documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic within five years of joining.

What about a baby born after I join?

Children who become members at birth are excepted from the congenital condition limitation.

item.description: CrowdHealth costs $60/mo per person plus a capped crowd contribution. Worst case is $200/mo under 55, $340 at 55-64, $660 for a family of four. Real math.
item.content:encoded:
In short: CrowdHealth costs $60 a month per person, children included, plus a crowd contribution that's hard-capped by age and household. Under 55 your worst possible month is $200. From 55 to 64 it's $340. For a family of four or more it's $660. On top of that you cover the first $500 of any health event. The crowd usually asks for less than the cap.

Every time somebody asks me what CrowdHealth costs, I give them a number, and then I watch them not believe it. So let me do this the long way, with the arithmetic in the open.

My family of four has been on it since 2022. Here's exactly how the money works.

The three pieces

One. The subscription: $60 a month, per person.

Children count. A family of four pays $240 a month in subscription. This is the part that doesn't move. It pays for the app, the people who negotiate your bills down, and a Care Advocate you can actually reach.

It does not go up because you got older, and it does not go up because you got sick.

Two. The crowd contribution: variable, but capped.

Each month you chip in to fund other members' bills. That's the crowdfunding part, and it's the number people worry about, because "variable" sounds like "unlimited."

It isn't. There's a published ceiling.

Three. The member commitment: $500 per health event.

A health event is one thing that happens to you. A broken wrist. An appendix. You cover the first $500 of it, and the crowd covers the eligible rest. It works like a deductible, except it resets per event instead of per year, and it's $500 instead of five figures.

The cap, which is the part nobody tells you

Who you areMost the crowd can ask in one monthYour worst case, with the $60
Ages 0 to 54$140$200 per person
Ages 55 to 64$280$340 per person
A family of four or more$420 for the whole household$660 for the family

Read the bottom row twice. A family of four pays $240 in subscription, and the crowd can ask for at most $420 more. Six hundred sixty dollars is the worst month that family can possibly have. Then $500 on top if somebody actually gets hurt that month.

That's the ceiling. It is not the normal month. CrowdHealth has historically not asked for the full amount, and in a quiet month the ask is a good bit lower.

For a real month: in October 2026, CrowdHealth told members the all-in cost was $165 for a single member under 55, $270 for a single member 55 or older, and $555 for a family of four, before a small transaction fee.

One change is already announced. On January 1, 2027, the subscription goes from $60 to $65 per person. If the crowd caps stay where they are, the worst cases become $205, $345, and $680. I'll update this page when the 2027 caps are published.

Let's do it for real people

A 35-year-old on her own. $60 subscription. Worst month, $200. If she breaks an ankle in March, add $500 that one time. Her worst possible year, assuming the crowd maxed her out every single month and she got hurt once, is $2,400 plus $500, so $2,900.

Now price a bronze marketplace plan for a 35-year-old without a subsidy. The premium alone often beats $2,900 before the deductible does one thing for her.

A 58-year-old bridging to Medicare. $60 subscription, but his cap is $280, so his worst month is $340 and his worst year is $4,080 plus commitments. That's a real step up from the under-55 number, and I'm not going to pretend it isn't. Then go price an individual plan for a 58-year-old. It's frequently north of a thousand dollars a month. The gap is still enormous. More on that in health sharing for early retirees.

A family of four, two adults under 55. $240 subscription. Worst month $660. Worst year $7,920, before any $500 commitments.

Compare that to a family plan with a $1,500 monthly premium and a $12,000 deductible, which is $18,000 before the plan pays for anything. That comparison is why we switched.

Where the savings actually come from

It isn't magic, and it isn't the crowd being generous. Two things do the work.

Cash prices. When you walk in as self-pay instead of insured, the price is often dramatically lower for the identical service. Discounts commonly run 25 to 85 percent off billed charges. CrowdHealth's team negotiates this for you before the crowd ever sees the bill, which means the crowd is funding a smaller number. I wrote about the mechanism in why cash prices beat insured prices.

Aligned incentives. CrowdHealth makes its money on that flat $60, not on a slice of your claims. Nobody there gets a bonus for slow-walking your bill. That's the whole argument in nobody gets paid to make you well.

What the price does not buy you

I'd be selling you something if I stopped here.

The low number is low partly because you're giving something up, and it's a real thing. There is no legal guarantee your bill gets funded. CrowdHealth is not insurance. No state insurance regulator can step in for you if a bill goes unfunded.

The funding rate is 99.8 percent across 53,877 bills, which is a strong record. A record is not a promise, and I won't dress it up as one.

You're also not buying coverage for a condition you already have. Anything documented, diagnosed, or symptomatic within five years of joining gets nothing in years one and two, then up to $25,000 a year from year three. High cholesterol and high blood pressure are exempt. If that rule lands on you, the cheap monthly number is beside the point.

The full picture, including who should walk away, is on my CrowdHealth guide.

So is it cheaper?

For a reasonably healthy household with a cushion, on our numbers, by a lot.

For somebody with an ongoing condition, or somebody getting a large ACA subsidy, quite possibly not. Run your own numbers before you cancel anything, and read who health sharing is wrong for first.

$60 per person in subscription, children included, plus a capped crowd contribution. Worst case all in is $200 a month under 55, $340 from 55 to 64, and $660 for a family of four or more. Most months come in under the cap.

The $60 subscription is the same at any age. The cap is not. It's $140 up to 54 and $280 from 55 to 64, so crossing 55 moves your worst month from $200 to $340.

No. There's a $500 member commitment per health event instead, and it resets per event rather than per year.

How much does CrowdHealth cost for a family?

$60 per person, so $240 for a family of four, plus a household crowd cap of $420. That's $660 in the worst month.

Yes, and it's published by age and household size. That cap is the direct answer to the usual objection that crowdfunding has no out-of-pocket maximum. On the monthly side, it does.
